Smoke, and probably "vape" "vapor" as well, is an aerosol. Which means it is solid and liquid particles suspended in air. Not an actual gas or vapor. I expect that even in a totally sealed container, you would have the liquids condense out on the walls of the container, trap the solid particles, and create a residue (though it would take a lot of smoke) on the inside of the container.

Those solid particles only have two places to go... diffuse through the air in the bottle (and leak out if the bottle isn't sealed) and condensing on the walls of the container.

The smoke/solids are heavier than the air they are in, so will tend to settle if there is no wind / convective current. Any diffusal that happens at the boundary layer obviously wouldn't change the make-up in the main body of the smoke. If a smoke particle were ejected from the main body of the smoke, its place would be taken by another particle, like if you removed a marble from the bottom of a jar. In the case of condensing on the walls of the jar, since the residue is so much denser than the smoke itself, a little residue eats a LOT of smoke. So it's equivalent of a marble disappearing. The rest of the smoke particles will fall into the space created, since they are heavier than the air in the jar.

I'm not a scientist. But pretty sure vape "vapor" is actually an aerosol... Might help to think of it as water with a bunch of slightly-heavier-than-water particles in it.
